Unfortunately, due to the safety challenges associated with hydrogen gas, it is an increasingly difficult to source process technology. Alternatively, vacuum furnace technology has continuously improved over the decades and the resulting high gradient performance between vacuum and hydrogen brazed components is often indistinguishable. Regardless of the process used, brazing has a few significant advantages compared to fusion-based joining methods such as electron beam welding. Firstly: there is very little thermal deformation of the final assembly, as the parts are heated and cooled uniformly and thus are less susceptible to distort. During welding, there is significant localized heating, which leads to localized thermal expansion and contraction, resulting in the increased potential for component deformation. Often, this thermal deformation can be minimized through a combination of proper weld joint design, appropriate welding technology and optimized welding sequences. During brazing, a multimeter long AS can be stacked vertically with self-locating registration features such that the central cell axis can be very precisely aligned. For reference, the straightness of the beam axis for 1.8m long C-band structure designs for an FEL application are ±50 µm while the X-band straightness would require 1 ASTM F68 Standard Specification for Oxygen-Free Copper in Wrought Forms for Electron Devices Page 2 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program ±10 µm over 1.8 m [1]. Achieving this straightness tolerance with split cell structures, is fundamentally challenging primarily due to the soft temper of the copper bodies after the brazing processes and the corresponding deformations which can occur without extreme handling vigilance. This risk can be partially mitigated through transport and support fixturing and structure body design, however the rectangular cross- section with the thinnest dimension experiencing gravity, lifting and shock/vibrational forces during transportation make the topology more sensitive than cylindrical axial coupled or boxier side coupled structures. Besides issues of thermal deformation, brazing also has the advantage that multiple hermitic joints can be formed during a single brazing operation and economies of scale can be realized when brazing multiple structures in the same furnace. For example, the roughly 100+ cells used in the Spring8, SwissFEL and ELI- NP structure can be joined in a single brazing cycle, assuming a sufficiently tall vertical brazing oven.
